Some of the birth-stories arc evidently ButHhbiUc and entirely 
depend for their point on some custom or idea peculiar to Buddhism ; 
but many are pieces of folk-lore which have floated about the world

in the course of their long wanderings, come to l>e recognised under

Jatakns or Birth-stories, which am arranged in 22 nipiUa* or books. 
This division is roughly founded on the number of verses (p&bu) 
which are quoted in each story; lliue the first book contains 
150 stories, each of which only quotes one verse, the second 100, each 
of which quotes two, the third and fourth 50 each, which respectively

which quotes B0 verses, and the twenty-second with 10 stories, each 
quoting a still larger number. Each story opens with b preface 
the ptrrouppuamisattAu or ‘story of the present', which rafale* 
the particular circumstances in the Buddha's life which led him to 
tell the birth-story and thus reveal *<>mc event in Lhe long series 
of hia previous existences as a tafitiMtfe or a being destined to attain 
Buddha-ship. At the ond there is always given n short summary, 
where the Buddha identifies the different actors in the story in tbeir 
present births at the time of hia discourse,— it being on essential 
condition of the book tlmt the Buddha pos&e^es Lhe same power as 
that which Pythagoras claimed but with a far more extrusive range, 
since he could remain ber all the past events in every being's previous 
existences it well us in hi* own. Every story ts also illustrated by 
one or more gtiihTta which are uttered by the Buddha while still a 
BodhU&tu and so playing lus part in the narrative; but sometimes 
the verses are put into his mouth as the Buddha, when they are

handed down from very early times in the Buddhist community, it i* 
not a question of much importance except for Pali literary history. 
The gtithas are undoubtedly old, and they necessarily imply the 
previous existence of the stories, though not perhaps in the exact 
words in which we lifiw posses them.

The ijirtakns are preceded in the PiLli text by a long Introduction, 
the hfidaim-kalha, which gives the Buddha’s previous history both 
before his last birth, aim also during bis last existence until ho 
attained the state of a Buddha’. This has been translated by Professor 
Rhys Davids, hut ns it baa no direct connexion with the rest of the 
work, we have omitted it in our translation, which commences with 
the first Birth-story.We have translated the quasi historical introductions which 
always precede the different birth-stories, as they are an essential 
part of the plan of the original work,—since they link each tale with 
some special incident in the Buddha's life, which tradition venerates 
as the occasion when ho is supposed to have recalled the forgotten 
scene of a long past existence to his contemporaries But it b an 
interesting question for future investigation how far they contain any 
historical data. They appear at first sight to harmonise with the 
framework <>f the Pi takas; lint I confess that 1 have on confidence in 
their historical credibility,—-they seem to me rather the laboured 
invention of a later age, like the legendary history of the early 
centuries of ancient Rome. But this question will be more easily 
settled, when we have mode farther progress in the tmhslaitoii.

The Ja takas themselves are of course interesting an specimens 
of Buddhist literature; but their foremost interest to us consists in 
their relation to folk-lore and the Light which they often throw on 
those popular stones which illustrate sc vividly the ideas and 
superstitions of the early rimes of civilisation. In this respect, they 
possess a special value, as, although much of their matter is peculiar 
to Rmlilbinm, they contain embedded with it au unrivalled collection 
of Folk-lore They are also full of interest as giving a vivid picture 
of the social life and customs of ancient India, Such books us 
Lieutenant-Colonei Sleetnan's 1 Rambles ' or Mr GHereon a 4 Bihar 
Peasant Life' illustrate them »t every turn. They form in fret an 
ever-shifting panorama of the village life such as Fah-bian and 
Riouea-thsnng saw it in the old days before the Muhammadan
